## Mara Vell (protagonist) — also called Mara
Who: Nineteen, the new keeper of Grayhallow's harbor light. Practical, stubborn, quietly funny.
Voice: Short sentences. Deflects with dry jokes. Never says 'please' when she can say 'now'.
Wants: Keep the light, keep Pip fed, and find out what her father hid.

## Theo Brandt (supporting)
Who: Harbor clerk, twenty-six. Precise, polite, and secretly in debt to the Calloway Shipping Company.
Voice: Formal and careful; over-qualifies everything. Turns blunt only when frightened.

## Pip Vell (supporting) — also called Pip
Who: Mara's eleven-year-old brother. Collects knots, lies badly, notices everything.

"Nothing. Go to bed."

"It's half past six."

"Then go to bed early. It'll be a novelty." She closed the ledger and set her palm on it, as if it might open again on its own. "Did Dad ever take anything out of here? Pages?"

Pip's hands stopped. It was only for a second, and then the cord was moving again, over and under, but Mara had raised him since he was four and she knew what his hands did when he was deciding whether to lie.

"Pip."

"He said not to tell you."

The light swung over them, and the room went white, and then grey.

"He's dead," Mara said, more gently than she felt. "I think the rule went with him."

Pip looked at the cord instead of her. "He burned them. In the stove. Last winter. He said some things are better kept by the sea."

"That sounds like him."

"He was crying," Pip said. "A bit."

Mara didn't say anything to that. She didn't trust what would come out.

The harbor office was warm and smelled of ink and wet wool, and Theo Brandt was the only one left in it, as he usually was. He stood when she came in. He always stood, as though she were someone.

"Miss Vell. Is something wrong with the light?"

"The light's fine. I need the shipping registers. Last October."

He took off his spectacles, cleaned them on a handkerchief that did not need it, and put them back on. "May I ask why?"

"You may ask."

That got the corner of his mouth, a little. "The registers belong to the harbor board. I would need a reason that I could, ah, write down. If anyone asked. Which they would not. Probably."

"My father kept a record of every ship that passed the light for twenty years," Mara said. "And he cut out October. I want to know what passed in October."

Theo was quiet for long enough that she heard the clock. Then he said, very carefully, "The Constance went down in October."

"I know that. Everyone knows that."

"Then you know the Calloway Company paid the families." He looked at the door, though no one was there. "And that they would not be pleased to hear anyone asking about it again."

"Are you going to tell them?"

"No," Theo said. He said it too quickly, and then he looked as if he would like to take it back and say it slower. "No. Come tomorrow, after six. I'll have them out."

"Why not now?"

"Because Mr. Calloway's man comes for the post at seven," Theo said, "and I would rather he didn't find you reading his business." He paused. "Bring a lamp. The archive has no windows, and I'm told I am poor company in the dark."

Mara buttoned her coat to the throat and went back out into the fog. Behind her she heard him lock the door, and then, after a moment, lock it again.
